The correct answer is true because it is the last stage of translocation and this process is called termination. At the end of translocation, the empty tRNA molecule is released from the E site and the ribosome moves downstream along mRNA to accept a new tRNA molecule from the P site. This cycle continues until the ribosome reaches a stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA), which does not encode for any amino acid. At this point, the empty tRNA molecule in the P site leaves the ribosome, triggering the release factors to dissociate from the ribosome. The polypeptide chain is then released from the ribosome. The next step is the process of translation elongation. In the elongation cycle, the ribosome will move along mRNA to the next codon and repeat the same process as above. The main purpose of releasing the tRNA molecules at the end of each cycle is to ensure the continuous working of translocation. If the tRNAs are not released, they will be stuck on the ribosomes and will cause many problems. Firstly, there is no space for more tRNAs to bind with the ribosome. Secondly, if the ribosome has too much tRNAs, it would be heavy and hard to move around. Thirdly, if the proteins are still attached to the ribosome after being synthesised, they will be unable to perform their functions. Therefore, it is very important to release the tRNAs at the end of each cycle so that the ribosome can continue to do its job.
